blocks.text: Bondi has a rhythm, and the quickest way to enjoy your day here is to fall into step with it. The etiquette isn't complicated — swim between the red and yellow flags, keep your music to yourself, take your rubbish home, and remember the beach belongs to everyone. Get those right and you'll blend in like you've been coming for years. Here's how we actually do things on our patch of sand.

items.label: Golden rule
items.value: Swim between the red & yellow flags

items.label: Alcohol
items.value: Not permitted on the beach or in Bondi Park

items.label: Dogs
items.value: Not allowed on the beach at any time

items.label: Smoking & vaping
items.value: No — keep it off the sand

items.label: Rubbish
items.value: Bin it or take it with you

blocks.text: Safety first: swim between the flags

If you take one thing from this whole guide, make it this. The red and yellow flags mark the patrolled swimming area, and the lifeguards set them where it's safest on any given day — which changes constantly with the surf and the rips. Swim between them and you're in the eyes of the professionals who've made Bondi famous. Wander outside them and you're on your own, often right where the rips run. Surfers, meanwhile, stay well clear of the flagged zone; boards and swimmers don't mix.

blocks.title: Respect the lifeguards
blocks.text: The lifeguards are here to keep everyone safe, so follow their instructions without argument — if they wave you in or move the flags, there's a reason. If they're busy and can't stop for a chat, don't take it personally. Their job comes before conversation.

New to ocean swimming or travelling with kids? North Bondi, near the flags at the northern end, tends to be gentler and shallower, which is why families cluster there. It's also where the surf school and the kids' pool area sit.
Bondi gets packed in summer, and the unwritten rules are really just common courtesy dialled up for a crowd. A few that matter most:
Leave the speaker at home. There's nowhere on this beach your playlist won't carry, and the person next to you didn't come to hear it. Headphones if you must.
Choose your spot with the crowd in mind. If you want breathing room, the middle of the beach or the southern end gives you more space than the busy northern corner near the flags.
Set up your tent or umbrella from the midpoint toward the back of the beach so you're not blocking anyone's view of the water — and if someone parks in front of you, let it go. It's a public beach.
Be sun smart. That first-day-in-Australia sunburn is brutal and entirely avoidable. Our UV is fierce even on cool days, so slip, slop, slap and reapply.
Watch out for the little ones. There are kids everywhere in summer, darting in and out — keep an eye out when you're moving around, throwing a ball or bodysurfing in.
The things that'll actually get you in trouble

Some Bondi rules aren't just etiquette — they're enforced by Waverley Council, and rangers do patrol. Alcohol is not permitted on Bondi Beach or in Bondi Park; the area sits within the council's alcohol-free and alcohol-prohibited zones, so leave the esky drinks at home. Smoking and vaping don't belong on the sand either. And dogs are not allowed on Bondi Beach at any time, though you're welcome to walk them on a lead along the promenade and through the park.

blocks.title: Parking: don't risk the big fine
blocks.text: After circling for a park it's tempting to chance it — don't. Blocking a driveway or a no-parking zone can land you a hefty fine and, if you box someone in, a call to the police. And please don't idle at the car park entrance waiting for a spot to open; it gridlocks Campbell Parade and makes everyone's day worse.
Rules and specifics can change, so if you're unsure about alcohol zones, dog areas or seasonal restrictions, the Waverley Council beach pages are the source of truth — I've linked them below.

Beyond the official stuff, there's the Bondi finishing school. Take your rubbish with you — bins line the promenade, so you're never more than a short walk from one, and the gulls and the ocean will thank you. Don't hover in the car park stalking someone's spot. If you've left a pram in the North Bondi rack, double-check you're grabbing your own before you wheel off; there are always dozens of near-identical black prams, and a mix-up ruins two families' afternoons.
The whole ethos is simple: the beach isn't here to watch you, it's here for everyone. Come to have fun, not to be seen.

items.q: Can you drink alcohol on Bondi Beach?
items.a: No. Bondi Beach and Bondi Park fall within Waverley Council's alcohol-free and alcohol-prohibited zones, so drinking on the sand or in the park isn't allowed and rangers do enforce it. Check the Waverley Council website for the exact zones and current rules.

items.q: Are dogs allowed on Bondi Beach?
items.a: Dogs aren't permitted on Bondi Beach at any time. You can walk a dog on a lead along the promenade and through the park, and there's an off-leash area at nearby Marks Park, a short walk south toward Tamarama.

items.q: Why does everyone say to swim between the flags?
items.a: The red and yellow flags mark the area the lifeguards patrol and have judged safest that day. Bondi is famous for its rips, which shift with the conditions, so swimming between the flags keeps you in the safest water and in the lifeguards' line of sight.

items.q: Can you smoke or vape on Bondi Beach?
items.a: Keep it off the sand — smoking and vaping aren't welcome on the beach. It's both an etiquette and a health issue on a crowded family beach, and butts are a genuine pollution problem for the ocean.

items.q: What's the most common tourist mistake at Bondi?
items.a: Two stand out: getting badly sunburnt on day one because the Australian UV is far stronger than most visitors expect, and swimming outside the flags. Sort those and you're already ahead of most first-timers.
